title: SubTrack your Grad: Gradient Subspace Tracking for Memory and Time Efficient Full-Parameter LLM Training (arXiv 2502.01586v1; the slug says SubTrack++, but the local file is the v1 SubTrack-Grad paper)
sections_read: 3. SubTrack-Grad: Tracking the Gradient Subspace (incl. Eq. 1-6, Algorithm 1)
4. Theoretical Analysis (Def. 4.1 L-continuity, Thm 4.2 Convergence, Def. 4.3 Exponential Map, Def. 4.4 Stiefel Manifold, Def. 4.5 Grassmann Manifold, Thm 4.6 Grassmann Exponential)
5. Experiments and Results: Time and Space Complexity
5. Experiments and Results: Reducing Optimization Jumps
Appendix A. Convergence of SubTrack-Grad (proof of Thm 4.2)
Appendix B. Grassmann Exponential (proof of Thm 4.6, Def. B.1 Orthogonal Group)

setup.task_type: Optimizer efficiency. No activations, no interpretability, no knowledge/behaviour analysis. The object being tracked is the low-rank subspace of each weight matrix's GRADIENT during training.
setup.data: Fine-tuning: GLUE (CoLA, STS-B, MRPC, RTE, SST-2, MNLI, QNLI, QQP) and SuperGLUE (BoolQ, CB, COPA, WIC, WSC, AXg). Pre-training: C4 for 10K iterations.
setup.models_with_sizes: RoBERTa-Base (GLUE, ranks 4 and 8), RoBERTa-Large (SuperGLUE, rank 8); Llama-style architectures of 60M, 130M, 350M, 1B and 3B parameters trained from scratch (ranks 128/256/256/512/512; Table 14 gives hidden 512-4096, layers 8-32). Parameter counts of RoBERTa models are not stated in the paper.
setup.positions_layers_read: Not applicable: every weight matrix's m x n gradient is projected onto a rank-r subspace (left singular vectors if m <= n, else right). No per-layer reporting.
setup.method: Initialise subspace by SVD of the first gradient; every k steps solve least squares A = argmin ||S A - G||, residual R = G - S A (in the orthogonal complement of S), tangent vector -2 R A^T, keep its rank-1 approximation, and step along the Grassmannian geodesic with step size eta (Eq. 6), which keeps S orthonormal.
setup.baselines: Full-Rank Adam, GaLore (periodic SVD of the gradient), BAdam (block coordinate descent).
setup.controls: All shared hyperparameters equal across methods; wall-time measured over a fixed number of subspace updates (5 for fine-tuning, 10 for pre-training) with evaluation steps excluded; NVIDIA A100 40GB; update-interval sweep 50-500 (Fig. 4, Table 15); toy 2D Ackley-function comparison (Fig. 3). No seeds or error bars reported.

key_results.claim: Wall-time savings vs GaLore in fine-tuning.
key_results.quote: SubTrack-Grad reduces wall-time by up to 20.57% on GLUE tasks (15% average reduction) and up to 65% on SuperGLUE tasks (22% average reduction) compared to GaLore.

key_results.claim: At 3B pre-training, GaLore's overhead is +157% vs full-rank and SubTrack's +31% (consistent with Table 6).
key_results.quote: Notably, for a 3B parameter model, GaLore incurred a substantial 157% increase in wall-time compared to full-rank training, whereas SubTrack-Grad exhibited a 31% increase

key_results.claim: Task performance is comparable to GaLore despite rank-1 subspace updates (true for fine-tuning; pre-training loss is slightly worse, Table 3).
key_results.quote: Despite limiting updates to rank-1 modifications of the previous subspace, SubTrack-Grad achieves superior or comparable performance compared to GaLore.
Additionally, the memory required for storing optimizer states in SubTrack-Grad, is equivalent to GaLore's.

key_results.claim: Frequent subspace updates are cheap for SubTrack but expensive for GaLore (Fig. 4, Table 15).
key_results.quote: GaLore's runtime significantly increases with more frequent subspace updates, whereas SubTrack-Grad maintains minimal overhead.

key_results.claim: Single-snapshot SVD re-estimation causes optimization jumps on a toy function (Fig. 3).
key_results.quote: These jumps prevent GaLore from reaching the global minimum within 100 steps when the scale factor is set to 1.

key_results.claim: Partial (block) updates hurt performance, more so at larger scale.
key_results.quote: its inability to update all the parameters simultaneously has caused performance loss, and the loss gets greater as the model size increases.

methods.name: Grassmannian subspace tracking with a rank-1 geodesic step (SubTrack-Grad update, Eq. 3-6, Algorithm 1)
methods.what_it_measures: How the dominant rank-r subspace of a sequence of matrices moves: fit the new matrix by least squares in the current subspace, take the residual in the orthogonal complement, form the tangent vector, and step along the geodesic. Quote: 'The tangent vector ∇F provides the direction for adjusting the subspace by accounting for the error lying in the orthogonal complement.' The size of that tangent or of the step is a rotation-speed signal.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: Only if adapted from gradients to activations: 5 transformed (the correct-answer subspace rotates between layers, tokens, or pressure conditions but keeps its energy) vs 6 erased (energy in the subspace and its rotated neighbourhood collapses into the residual). Also direction 3 (jump vs drift) via the per-step rotation profile.
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: None directly. It can pick candidate layers or tokens (largest rotation) where patching or ablation should be tried.
methods.data_and_compute_needed: Cheap: O(mnr) per update (Table 5). For us, stacked activations (items x d_model) per layer or token for a few hundred items; no GPU beyond activation extraction.
methods.code_available: Not stated in the paper (no repository link in the text).

methods.name: SVD-based subspace (GaLore baseline): re-estimate the subspace from scratch by SVD of one matrix
methods.what_it_measures: The top-r singular subspace of a single snapshot.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: Same as above, but the paper argues it is noise-sensitive and produces jumps; it is a cautionary baseline for us.
methods.code_available: GaLore is a separate public method; not provided by this paper.

methods.name: Memory-efficient full-parameter training via projected optimizer states
methods.what_it_measures: Not a measurement: it reduces Adam state memory from 2mn to mr + 2nr per matrix.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: None. Relevant only to Stage B cost (full-parameter DPO or fate-matched fine-tuning on 9B-27B).
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: Allows full-parameter rather than LoRA fine-tuning under a memory limit, so a 'fix' can touch all weights.
methods.data_and_compute_needed: Tested only up to 3B pre-training (10K iterations) and RoBERTa fine-tuning on an A100 40GB; never on DPO or 7B+ instruction models.

methods.name: Toy optimization-path visualization on the Ackley function

controls_worth_copying: When comparing two subspace-estimation procedures, fix the number of update events (here exactly 5 or 10 subspace updates) so costs are comparable, and exclude evaluation steps from timing.
Sweep the update frequency (interval 50-500, Table 15) and report both cost and outcome, rather than one setting.
Keep all shared hyperparameters identical across methods.
For our use: compare a smoothed (tracked) subspace with an unsmoothed per-layer SVD subspace; if they disagree on where a jump is, the jump may be noise.

pitfalls.pitfall: A subspace estimated by SVD of a single matrix is noise-sensitive; for us, subspaces from a few hundred items per layer will jitter, and adjacent-layer 'jumps' may be noise.
pitfalls.quote: Moreover, applying SVD to a single gradient matrix is susceptible to data noise (Vaswani et al., 2018)

pitfalls.pitfall: Not all layers have a stable subspace (cited claim, not shown here); one subspace per model is not safe.
pitfalls.quote: This is problematic because not all layers' gradients converge to a stable subspace early in training (Jaiswal et al., 2024).

pitfalls.pitfall: Higher-rank geodesic steps were unstable, so updates were restricted to rank-1. For diagnosis this design hides abrupt multi-dimensional changes: a tracker built to change slowly cannot detect a 'jump'.
pitfalls.quote: caused convergence issues in some cases. Therefore, we restricted updates to rank-1 in this paper

pitfalls.pitfall: Full-rank SVD of a tangent with tiny singular values hurts convergence.
pitfalls.quote: using the full-rank SVD of the tangent vector from (5), can hinder convergence if the singular values of the tangent vector become very small.

pitfalls.pitfall: The convergence proof assumes the subspace never changes, so it gives no guarantee for the tracking itself.
pitfalls.quote: This is where the constant subspace assumption becomes necessary.

pitfalls.pitfall: Step size trades tracking against stability; a decaying step size stops tracking.
pitfalls.quote: However, a decreasing step size can impair the ability to accurately track and adapt to subspace changes.

pitfalls.pitfall: Short pre-training budget: models are not converged, so pre-training comparisons are weak.
pitfalls.quote: this setup was sufficient for comparing methods rather than creating perfectly optimized models.

pitfalls.pitfall: Not stated by authors: the step size is tuned per task from 0.001 to 50 (Tables 12-13), the abstract's 'up to 20.57% on GLUE' is not reproducible from Table 8 (largest per-task reduction about 23.7%), no seeds or error bars are given, and pre-training loss is slightly worse than GaLore (Table 3).

limitations_quote: In some cases, the extent of changes in the subspace may require updates of ranks greater than 1; the pre-training of Llama-based architectures is a clear example of this need.
future_work_quote: In future work, we plan to explore increasing the rank of updates without compromising convergence.

bears_on_fates.how: The geodesic/tangent machinery (or plain principal angles between per-layer subspaces) could measure how far the correct-answer subspace rotates between layers, tokens, or pushback vs no-pushback. A small rotation that keeps the energy fits 'transformed'. This is my extrapolation; the paper only tracks gradients.

The residual R = G - S A (energy outside the tracked subspace) is a natural erasure measure: erasure means projected energy collapses with no nearby rotated subspace to absorb it. Extrapolation; not tested.
Projected-optimizer training could make full-parameter fine-tuning (plain DPO or fate-matched) on 9B-27B fit in memory, but the paper tests nothing above 3B and no preference training.

bears_on_group_angle: Helps: a worked, cheap recipe for following a rank-r subspace through a sequence of matrices on the Grassmannian. It fits the current subspace by least squares, takes the residual in the orthogonal complement, builds a tangent vector, and steps along a geodesic that keeps the basis orthonormal ('This update rule preserves the orthonormality of St+1 , ensuring it remains on the Grassmannian.', p. 4). For us the sequence index would be layer or token, and the matrix would be stacked activations or flipped-minus-resisted differences. The per-step rotation gives a profile across depth, and a spike is a candidate fork point; this maps onto direction 3 (jump vs drift). Warnings: (1) single-snapshot SVD subspaces are noisy and jump, so we need bootstrap or label-permutation noise floors before calling a jump real; (2) SubTrack-style smoothing with the previous subspace and rank-1 steps deliberately suppresses abrupt change, so it would bias a jump-vs-drift test toward 'drift'. For diagnosis, prefer unsmoothed principal angles between independently estimated subspaces plus a noise floor, and use tracking only for denoising. Nothing in the paper touches activations.
architecture_location: Nothing about where information lives. The method is applied independently to each weight matrix's gradient; there is no per-layer, per-component, or depth analysis of subspace behaviour. The only layer-level statement is cited from Jaiswal et al. (2024), not shown. Efficiency results cover Llama 60M-3B and RoBERTa-Base/Large, single runs with no seeds reported, so there is nothing on consistency across models or seeds beyond the efficiency trend.
actionable_fix: No fix for any fate follows from this paper. Indirect uses: (a) a monitor, i.e. a Grassmannian-distance or principal-angle profile of the correct-answer subspace across layers, to localise where it rotates or collapses before running patching; (b) for Stage B, GaLore/SubTrack-style projected optimizer states could allow full-parameter DPO on 9B-27B under a memory limit (optimizer memory mr+2nr vs 2mn, Table 4). This is untested for DPO or for models above 3B, and LoRA-DPO is the cheaper standard. The authors also speculate that low-rank optimization 'may also serve as a regularizer' (p. 9), which could change what a fine-tuning fix does compared with full fine-tuning.
reuse_verdict: adapt (math only): borrow the Grassmannian geodesic, tangent and principal-angle formulas (about 20 lines) as a subspace-motion measure across layers or tokens with a noise floor. Avoid the optimizer itself for diagnosis, and do not rely on its rank-1 smoothing, which hides jumps.
relevance_to_project: Low, lower than the title suggests. This is an optimizer-efficiency paper about gradient subspaces during training; it never looks at activations, knowledge, behaviour under pressure, or interpretability, and says nothing about architecture location. Its only value for us is the Grassmannian subspace math and the warning that single-snapshot SVD subspaces are noisy and jump. Note: the local file is v1 ('SubTrack your Grad'), not the SubTrack++ version the slug names, so later additions in ++ are not covered.
